questions.prompt: In mass wasting, soil and rock move down a slope, sometimes slowly and sometimes in a rush. Which force drives that downhill movement every time?
questions.accessiblePrompt: In mass wasting, soil and rock move down a slope, sometimes slowly and sometimes in a rush. Which force drives that downhill movement every time?

choices.text: Rainwater
choices.rationale: Rainwater makes slopes heavier and weaker, and it is part of a mudflow, but creep and rock falls also happen on dry slopes. Water is a trigger, not the force that drives every event.

choices.text: Gravity
choices.rationale: Correct. Gravity pulls earth material toward lower ground in every kind of mass wasting, from slow creep to sudden rock falls.

choices.text: Wind
choices.rationale: Wind can move dust and sand, but it cannot shove a hillside of soil and rock downhill.

choices.text: Friction
choices.rationale: Friction does the opposite job: it helps hold soil and rock in place until gravity overcomes it.

questions.explanation: Gravity is the engine of all mass wasting: it constantly pulls soil and rock toward lower ground. Water, earthquakes and digging can make a slope weaker or give it a jolt, but they act as triggers. Gravity is what actually moves the material downhill.
questions.misconception: Water or wind is what pushes soil and rock downhill; gravity only matters for things that fall through the air.
questions.hint: Ask what would still pull on a boulder sitting on a perfectly dry, windless hillside.

questions.prompt: Which conditions make a hillside more likely to have a fast mass-wasting event? Select all that apply.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Which conditions make a hillside more likely to have a fast mass-wasting event? Select all that apply. The choices are: a steep slope; soil soaked by several days of heavy rain; strong shaking from an earthquake; a long dry spell with no rain for several months; gentle, nearly flat ground.

choices.text: A steep slope
choices.rationale: Correct. The steeper the slope, the more of gravity's pull acts down the slope, so material moves more readily and faster.

choices.text: Soil soaked by several days of heavy rain
choices.rationale: Correct. Water adds weight and weakens the soil, and the lesson ties earthflows and mudflows to heavy rain.

choices.text: Strong shaking from an earthquake
choices.rationale: Correct. Shaking can break loose material on steep ground; the 2016 slide in Japan followed a strong earthquake.

choices.text: A long dry spell with no rain for several months
choices.rationale: On its own, a dry spell lowers the chance of a fast earthflow or mudflow, because dry soil is lighter and holds together better than soaked soil.

choices.text: Gentle, nearly flat ground
choices.rationale: With almost no slope, gravity has little downhill pull to work with, so flat ground has low mass-wasting potential.

questions.explanation: Steep slopes give gravity a better angle, soaked soil is heavier and weaker, and earthquake shaking can jar loose material that was barely holding on. Dry weather and gentle slopes work the other way, which is why mapped landslide risk is low on flat, dry ground.
questions.misconception: Only the steepness of a slope matters; rain and earthquakes do not change the odds of a landslide.
questions.hint: Think about what helps gravity win against the soil's grip, and what helps the soil hold on.

evidence.supports: Steep, wet slopes shed rock and soil faster than gentle, dry ones, and quakes in steep terrain commonly set off landslides.

evidence.locator: Section 2, Planning for Mass Wasting Events
evidence.supports: Slope steepness, earth material, weathering rate, earthquakes and human activity affect the chance of mass wasting.

evidence.title: Landslide Types and Processes (Fact Sheet 2004-3072)
evidence.supports: Slope saturation by water is a primary cause of landslides, and earthquakes in steep, landslide-prone areas greatly increase the likelihood that landslides will occur.

questions.hint: Look for the one clue in each description: very slow, lots of water, a cliff, or a large soggy mass.

items.text: A strong wall built at the foot of a steep hill
items.rationale: A wall at the bottom stops rock and soil that start moving, so it holds material back rather than dealing with water.

choices.text: A county shaded low risk on the same map will never flood

choices.text: Build X as it is, because it delivered the most data of the three
choices.rationale: X delivers 99% of its data, but its battery lasts only 3 months, far short of the 12 months required.

choices.text: Build Y as it is, because its battery outlasted the other two
choices.rationale: Y runs for 24 months, but it delivers only 82% of its data, well below the 95% required.

choices.text: Combine X's data link with Y's power system, then test it again
choices.rationale: Correct. X has the best data link and Y the best power system, so a design combining them could meet both requirements, and testing again checks that it really does.

choices.text: Build Z as it is, because it landed in the middle on both tests
choices.rationale: Z fails both requirements, with 88% of its data and 8 months of running time. Landing in the middle is not the same as meeting the criteria.

choices.text: Combine Z's data link with X's power system, then test it again
choices.rationale: Neither of these parts passed its requirement: Z's data link delivered 88% and X's power system lasted 3 months, so this design would likely fail both tests.

questions.conditions: Each prototype's data delivery depends on its data link and its running time depends on its power system, and parts from different prototypes can be fitted together.
questions.limitations: Parts that worked well separately can affect each other once they are joined, so a combined design must be tested again before it is trusted.
questions.explanation: None of the three prototypes meets both requirements: X passes the data test but its battery dies too soon, and Y lasts long enough but loses too much data. Because X's best feature and Y's best feature come from different parts, engineers can combine them into a new design, much as the DART team combined its best fixes. They still have to test it, because parts that worked separately can affect each other once they are joined.
questions.misconception: The prototype that wins one test is the best design overall, so engineers should just pick one prototype as it is.
questions.hint: Check each prototype against both requirements. Does any one of them pass both?
